forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

summary.summary: Covering report presenting Tandridge's draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025/26 — the annual self-assessment of governance that must be published alongside the accounts. The AGS itself and its 2026/27 action plan sit in appendices not included in this paper, which contains no financial figures.

news_drafts.headline: Tandridge investments forecast at £605,973 below capital value at 30 September, from £571,574 in March
news_drafts.lead:
Tandridge District Council's investments are forecast to stand £605,973 below their capital value at 30 September 2026, according to a market valuation report for its Investment Sub Committee, which met on 10 November. The deficit was £571,574 at 31 March 2026.

The table in the report, Appendix B, is headed as a forecast at 30 September rather than a final valuation. It gives the total as a deficit of £(605,973), compared with £(571,574) six months earlier.

The report attributes the deficit to two holdings, the Schroders Bond Fund and the CCLA Diversification Fund. The papers give no other figures for the period.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B - Market Value of Investments Sept 2026

news_drafts.headline: Tandridge's 2025/26 draft accounts met 30 June deadline; council due to be abolished 31 March 2027
news_drafts.lead:
Tandridge District Council's finance team published its 2025/26 draft accounts on the statutory deadline of 30 June 2026, months before the council is due to be abolished on 31 March 2027, the Audit & Scrutiny Committee's papers show. The papers call it "a fantastic achievement" for a small team that also handled Local Government Reorganisation and took over external audit arrangements (the independent check on the accounts) from Surrey County Council in April 2025. They note that many larger councils missed the deadline.

The 2024/25 accounts were signed off by auditors within statutory deadlines, the council's first full-scale audit since the pre-Covid year of 2018/19. For 2025/26, however, Grant Thornton, the external auditors, expects to issue a disclaimer, meaning it will not give an opinion on the accounts. The paper says the auditors have no assurance over balances brought forward from 2023/24, which were deprioritised in that year's audit. That leaves them unable to vouch for the movements in the year or the prior-year comparisons.

The council's replies to the auditors show how abolition is shaping its plans. Asked to find further recurring savings for its medium-term financial strategy (its multi-year spending plan), the council said its focus is on "financial sustainability to vesting day", the date functions pass to the successor East Surrey authority. It will deliver approved savings "where practicable", maintain reserves and avoid unnecessary pressures for the successor. On housing, it is engaging with the Regulator of Social Housing and developing an improvement plan after a C4 consumer standards grading.

The internal audit progress report lists seven overdue management actions. The business continuity audit of October 2025 gave "No" assurance, the lowest rating, after finding none of eight completed plans had been tested. Its high-priority action, due 30 April 2026, now has a revised date of "TBC". Others date back to a June 2024 asset management audit, where two low-priority actions are now due 30 October 2026.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - External Auditors Update October 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 6 Q2 2026-27 Budget Monitoring - Housing Services Committee use this one
findings.headline: The paper says a reserve exists to mitigate the impact of temporary accommodation costs on Housing Benefit.
findings.detail: The paper notes that the Homelessness budget is sensitive to temporary accommodation costs, and that these can have a knock-on impact on Housing Benefit. It says a reserve exists to mitigate the impact on Housing Benefit, but gives no figure in this extract.
findings.matters: A ring-fenced reserve for a volatile temporary accommodation cost is a risk-management arrangement that other councils would compare against their own homelessness exposure.
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation costs can also have a knock-on impact on Housing Benefit (although a reserve exists to mitigate the impact on the latter).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 6 Q2 2026-27 Budget Monitoring - Housing Services Committee use this one
findings.headline: Council tax on void properties adds £59k to HRA service costs, with the paper citing an increase in void council tax.
findings.detail: The paper reports a £58k overall services cost pressure, mainly from a £59k increase in council tax on void properties. This is partly offset by a £20k reduction in the Assisted Purchase Scheme, based on the number of ongoing applications.
findings.matters: Void council tax is a recurring cost to landlords that other councils with stock turnover would want to benchmark against.
findings.figures: £58k services cost overspend; £59k council tax on void properties; (£20k) Assisted Purchase Scheme reduction
findings.quote: Mainly due to £59k increase in Council tax on void properties

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 6 Q2 2026-27 Budget Monitoring - Housing Services Committee use this one
findings.headline: The Housing General Fund savings target of £5k is marked as on track.
findings.detail: The paper sets a Housing General Fund savings target of £5k for the Committee and records it as on track. It does not give further detail on the savings plan in the extract provided.
findings.matters: A small savings target being on track is a positive delivery signal, and other councils would compare how their housing savings plans are tracking.
findings.figures: £5k savings target; £5k marked as on track

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 6 Q2 2026-27 Budget Monitoring - Housing Services Committee use this one
findings.headline: The Housing General Fund reports a £34k overspend, mainly from a £17k reduction in Surrey County Council contribution to Home Improvement Agency costs.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the overspend mainly to Private Sector Enabling, including the reduced Surrey County Council contribution, an expected £13k increase in Mole Valley Partnership costs, and an £11k rise in Home Improvement Agency core contract costs. A £12k salaries underspend from a team vacancy partly offsets these.
findings.matters: Reduced county council contributions to shared housing services are a cost pressure other district councils in two-tier areas would want to compare.
findings.figures: £34k Housing General Fund overspend; £33k Private Sector Enabling; £17k reduction in Surrey County Council contribution; £13k Mole Valley Partnership increase; £11k Home Improvement Agency increase; (£12k) salaries
findings.quote: Housing General Fund overspend £34k mainly due to :-

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 6 Q2 2026-27 Budget Monitoring - Housing Services Committee use this one
findings.headline: The SHDF 2.2 scheme is reported as £96k over budget, with the paper saying some of this may be covered by government grant.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the overspend to additional works needed to bring outstanding properties to a C energy performance rating. It says some of this may be covered by government grant funding upon successful reconciliation of the claim.
findings.matters: A capital overspend that depends on grant reconciliation is an exposure other councils delivering decarbonisation funding would recognise.
findings.quote: Potentially some of this will be covered by Government Grant Funding upon successful reconciliation of claim.
